about: Aircraft comparison data for aircraft.html. Every aircraft is one certified variant, not a family. Values are canonical-unit numbers (m, m2, kg, kN, kW, L, ft, kt, nm, deg, psi, cm, m3); js/aircraft.js converts for display. Per-aircraft: 's' = specs, 'n' = per-field notes, '~' = field ids whose value is approximate/rounded. Add a field by adding one entry to 'fields' — the table, charts, units and search pick it up from there.
sources: Manufacturer type specifications and airport planning manuals (Bombardier CSP A-020/B-020/D-020, Embraer APM, Boeing D6-58329 series)
FAA/EASA Type Certificate Data Sheets (A21EA CL-600, A57NM EMB-135/145, A57NM/IM ERJ-170/190, T00001SE 777, 3A12 Cessna 172)
ICAO Doc 8643 (type designators, wake category); FAA AC 150/5300-13B (airplane design group)
Manufacturer press specifications for in-development types (777-9)
caveats: Weights, range and field length are configuration- and option-dependent. Each row here is one common certified configuration — named in the variant line — not the only one that exists.
Range is manufacturer-quoted at typical seating with standard reserves; it is not a flight-planning number.
Takeoff and landing field lengths are at max structural weight, sea level, ISA, dry, level runway.
Values marked ≈ are rounded, averaged across sources, or preliminary (in-development types).
Nothing here substitutes for the AFM, the POH or the operator's performance data.

groups.label: Identity & program
groups.note: What it is, who built it, and where it sits in the certification and ATC world.

groups.label: Dimensions
groups.note: External geometry. Airport compatibility lives here.

groups.label: Weights
groups.note: Structural limits. Every one of these is a certificated number.

groups.label: Powerplant
groups.note: Per-engine figures unless the label says total.

groups.label: Systems
groups.note: How the airplane is put together behind the panel.

groups.label: Derived ratios
groups.note: Computed from the rows above — nothing here is quoted from a manufacturer.

fields.d: ICAO Doc 8643 code — what goes in box 9 of the flight plan and what ATC automation sees.
FAA type rating designation. Variants sharing a rating fly on differences training, not a new rating.
L < 7 t · M 7–136 t · H > 136 t · J = A380. Sets the separation behind you.
AC 150/5300-13B group by wingspan and tail height — decides taxiway width, gate and separation standards.
By Vref at max landing weight: A < 91 · B 91–120 · C 121–140 · D 141–165 kt. Picks your line of approach minimums.
Rounded program deliveries. Exact counts differ between sources and reporting dates.
Last published manufacturer list price. Nobody pays list; it is a scale marker, not a transaction price.
Folding wingtips exist to keep a big wing inside a smaller gate box.
More sweep delays the drag rise, so it buys cruise Mach — and costs low-speed lift.
Maximum interior width, which is where the seat count per row is decided.
Manufacturer's typical two-class layout, or the common airline fit where that is what the type actually flies.
Certificated exit limit — the most people the doors and slides are approved to evacuate in 90 seconds.
The wings carry fuel, so weight above this has to be fuel — MZFW is a wing bending limit, not a runway limit.
Airplane, fluids and crew — everything that flies but does not pay.
At 0.803 kg/L (6.7 lb/US gal), the standard Jet A planning density.
Flat-rated static takeoff thrust at sea level, ISA. Reserve ratings (APR/bump) are higher.
Shaft power — how piston and turboprop engines are rated instead of thrust.
Air around the core ÷ air through it. High bypass = more thrust per kilo of fuel, and a much bigger fan.
True airspeed at typical cruise altitude and Mach.
Maximum operating Mach number.
Maximum operating indicated airspeed below the Mach crossover.
Manufacturer range at typical seating with standard reserves.
Balanced field at max takeoff weight, sea level, ISA, dry level runway.
At max landing weight, sea level, ISA, dry level runway.
Total for all engines at typical cruise weight and altitude — an operating average, not a certified figure.
Demonstrated in certification. Not a limit unless the AFM says it is.
Lower is a more comfortable cabin — and a heavier, stronger fuselage to hold the pressure.
span² ÷ wing area. High aspect ratio = less induced drag = better cruise efficiency, at the cost of a heavier, more flexible wing.
MZFW − OEW. Published 'max payload' can differ where the manufacturer quotes a different empty-weight basis.
MTOW ÷ wing area. High wing loading rides turbulence better and needs more runway.
Total static thrust ÷ MTOW weight. Airliners live between 0.25 and 0.35.
Usable fuel ÷ MTOW. The long-range airplanes are the ones that are mostly fuel at brake release.
Structural payload ÷ MTOW.
Single-class seats ÷ overall length — how efficiently the tube is used.
Cruise burn ÷ single-class seats. The number that makes big airplanes look good.
Cruise burn ÷ seats ÷ cruise speed × 100. Rough, cruise-only, ignores climb and taxi.

aircraft.name: CRJ200
aircraft.blurb: The airplane that invented the 50-seat regional jet market by stretching a business jet. The Challenger 600's fuselage grew two plugs, kept its 2.57 m cabin, and suddenly a hub could feed itself with jets instead of turboprops. Its economics died with cheap-fuel scope clauses: 50 seats to push through a 24-tonne airplane is a hard number to make work above $2/gal.

n.mtow: LR; the base 200 is 21,523 kg and the ER 23,133 kg

aircraft.name: CRJ700
aircraft.blurb: Not a stretched CRJ200 — a new wing with leading-edge slats, a lowered cabin floor and more engine. The slats are the point: they gave the 700 the field performance the 200 never had, which is why it works out of short, hot and high fields the CRJ200 struggles with.

n.oew: ER; varies several hundred kg by interior

aircraft.name: CRJ900
aircraft.blurb: The CRJ700 with 3.9 m more fuselage and the seat count US scope clauses settled on — 76. For a decade this and the E175 were the only two airplanes a US major could legally hand to a regional partner, and the pair of them ate the entire large-RJ market.

aircraft.name: CRJ1000
aircraft.blurb: The stretch too far for the US market — 100 seats put it outside every scope clause, so it sold almost entirely to Air Nostrum and HOP!. Sixty-odd airframes. A textbook case of an airplane whose market was defined by a labour contract rather than by aerodynamics.

n.mtow: ER; the basic CRJ1000 is 40,824 kg

aircraft.name: ERJ 145
aircraft.blurb: The CRJ200's opposite number, built on a slimmer fuselage — 2.10 m of cabin instead of 2.57, so the seats go 1-2 and everyone gets an aisle or a window. Narrower means less wetted area and less drag per seat, and it is the reason a smaller, less thirsty engine did the same job.

s.fcs: Hydro-mechanical, powered ailerons and rudder; manual elevator trim tab

aircraft.name: E170
aircraft.blurb: Embraer's clean-sheet answer to the question the ERJ could not answer: a real 2-2 cabin with no middle seat and a proper cargo hold, sized at 70 seats. The double-bubble fuselage and underwing engines are what separate the E-Jets from every rear-engined regional that came before.

s.fcs: Fly-by-wire (spoilers, rudder, elevator); mechanical aileron backup

n.fcs: The E-Jet's ailerons are cable-driven; the rest is fly-by-wire

aircraft.name: E175
aircraft.blurb: The E170 with two fuselage plugs, and the airplane that won the 76-seat war outright. Same wing, same engines, six more seats than the E170 and a cabin US passengers will pick over a CRJ900 every time — which is exactly why regional carriers kept ordering it a decade after its replacement was designed.

s.fcs: Fly-by-wire (spoilers, rudder, elevator); mechanical aileron backup

n.paxt: US scope-clause fit; 88 in single class
n.range: E175LR, 76 passengers; the AR reaches 2,000 nm
n.icao: E75L is the long-wing E175; short-wing airframes file E75S

aircraft.name: E190
aircraft.blurb: Where the E-Jet stops being a regional jet: a bigger wing, the CF34-10E, 100+ seats and enough range to fly transcontinental legs that no CRJ could touch. JetBlue and Air Canada flew it as a mainline airplane, not a feeder.

s.fcs: Fly-by-wire (spoilers, rudder, elevator); mechanical aileron backup

aircraft.name: E195-E2
aircraft.blurb: The current state of the art at this size: a new high-aspect-ratio wing, geared-turbofan PW1900Gs and 146 seats — a 20-year evolution of the same fuselage cross-section the E170 introduced. Too many seats for a US scope clause, which is why you see it at Azul and Binter and not at a Delta Connection gate.

n.range: STD; the higher-MTOW build reaches about 3,000 nm

aircraft.name: 777-200ER
aircraft.blurb: The airplane that proved a twin could own the North Atlantic and then the Pacific. Designed with airlines in the room and drawn entirely in CATIA — the first jetliner with no physical mock-up — and certified for 180-minute ETOPS out of the box, which is what actually killed the four-engine long-haul fleet.

s.cont: 32 LD-3 containers or 10 pallets, plus bulk
s.fcs: Full fly-by-wire with back-driven controls and artificial feel
s.elec: 2 × 120 kVA IDG + 2 × 20 kVA backup, 115 V AC

n.abreast: 10-abreast (3-4-3) is common in modern high-density economy
n.emodel: The -200ER was offered with all three engine makes; GE90 shown
n.price: 2018 list, last published before Boeing stopped quoting

aircraft.name: 777-200LR
aircraft.blurb: A 777-200 fuselage on the -300ER's wing, gear and engines, with up to three auxiliary tanks in the aft hold — an airplane built to fly further than any airliner ever has, and it does: 11,664 nm Hong Kong to London the wrong way round in 2005. Very few were sold, because almost nobody needs to trade that much payload for that much range.

s.cont: 32 LD-3 containers, less any auxiliary fuel tanks fitted
s.fcs: Full fly-by-wire with back-driven controls and artificial feel
s.elec: 2 × 120 kVA IDG + 2 × 20 kVA backup, 115 V AC

n.fuell: with all three optional auxiliary tanks

aircraft.name: 777-300ER
aircraft.blurb: The best-selling 777 and, for fifteen years, the default long-haul airplane of the world's big carriers — 838 of them. Raked wingtips, a strengthened wing, semi-levered main gear so the stretched tail clears on rotation, and the GE90-115B: 115,300 lbf from one engine, still the most powerful jet engine ever certified.

s.cont: 44 LD-3 containers or 14 pallets, plus bulk
s.fcs: Full fly-by-wire with back-driven controls and artificial feel
s.elec: 2 × 120 kVA IDG + 2 × 20 kVA backup, 115 V AC

n.abreast: 10-abreast (3-4-3) is the modern economy standard on this type

aircraft.name: 777F
aircraft.blurb: A 777-200LR airframe with a main-deck cargo door and no windows — the largest twin-engine freighter, and the one that finally beat the 747-400F on trip cost because two engines burn less than four. 102 tonnes of payload, and it is the reason a 747 freighter is now a niche airplane.

s.fcs: Full fly-by-wire with back-driven controls and artificial feel
s.elec: 2 × 120 kVA IDG + 2 × 20 kVA backup, 115 V AC

n.icao: The freighter shares the B77L designator with the 777-200LR

aircraft.blurb: The stretch of the -300ER with a composite wing so large it does not fit a Code E gate — hence the 3.5 m folding wingtips, an airliner first. Sixteen years of 777 experience in the wing and the GE9X, and seven years of certification delay: first flight January 2020, entry into service now expected 2027.

s.fcs: Full fly-by-wire with back-driven controls and artificial feel
s.elec: 2 × 120 kVA IDG + 2 × 20 kVA backup, 115 V AC

n.spanf: the wingtips fold on the ground so the airplane fits a 65 m (Code E) gate box
n.cabw: the 777X cabin was widened about 10 cm by thinning the sidewalls

aircraft.blurb: Here for scale: the single-aisle workhorse the regional jets feed and the wide-bodies hand off to. Nearly 5,000 built. Its fuselage cross-section is the 1958 707's, which is why the engines are flattened at the bottom and the airplane sits so low to the ground.

n.fcs: One of the last airliners you can fly with the hydraulics gone

aircraft.name: A220-300
aircraft.blurb: Bombardier's answer to what should have followed the CRJ — a clean-sheet 5-abreast airplane with geared turbofans and a composite wing — sold to Airbus for a dollar after a trade fight nearly killed it. It is the airplane the CRJ1000 was trying to be, twelve years later and with a generation better engines.

s.avionics: Collins Pro Line Fusion, five 15-inch displays

n.seatw: 18–19 in — the widest economy seat of any narrow-body
n.abreast: 2-3, so two of five seats are middles instead of three of six

aircraft.blurb: Here for contrast with the 777: a composite-barrel fuselage, no bleed air, 5,000 psi hydraulics and a cabin held at 6,000 ft instead of 8,000 — a systems-architecture bet as much as an aerodynamic one. Roughly the 777-200ER's mission on three-quarters of the weight.

s.elec: 4 × 250 kVA VFSG + 2 × 225 kVA APU, no-bleed architecture
s.avionics: Rockwell Collins, five large-format displays, HUD standard

n.hydp: 5,000 psi lets the actuators and the lines be smaller and lighter
n.cabalt: the composite barrel is what makes a 6,000 ft cabin structurally affordable

aircraft.name: Cessna 172S
aircraft.blurb: The other end of the scale, and the reason this table has a log axis on the charts. More 172s have been built than any other aircraft in history. Put its 11 m wingspan next to a 777-9's 71.75 m in the scale drawing and the comparison stops being a table and becomes a picture.

s.autoland: Not applicable — VFR/IFR to published minimums

n.vmo: VNE, not VMO — the 172 has no Mach limit to worry about
n.mach: equivalent Mach at cruise, for the table's sake
n.tofl: total distance over a 50 ft obstacle at sea level, ISA — not a balanced field
n.built: all 172 variants since 1956, the most-produced aircraft ever
